course: Daily Milk Sales: Dairy Herd System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Mastitis is the most costly disease for small-scale dairy farmers in Africa. It reduces milk yield, lowers milk quality, and can kill cows if not treated. A cow with mastitis may drop from 15 litres per day to 5 litres, and the milk may be unfit for sale. In Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, studies show that up to 40% of dairy cows have subclinical mastitis at any time. That means you lose money without even seeing sick cows. Mastitis is an infection of the udder, usually caused by bacteria entering through the teat canal. It happens when hygiene is poor, when milking is rough, or when cows lie in dirty, wet bedding. The disease comes in two forms: clinical and subclinical. Clinical mastitis shows clear signs: hot, swollen udder, clumpy or bloody milk, and a sick cow. Subclinical mastitis has no visible signs in the udder or milk, but a lab test (like the California Mastitis Test) will show it. Subclinical cases cause the biggest hidden lossesâup to 70% of total mastitis cost. Other health issues in dairy herds include foot rot, milk fever, and retained placenta. Foot rot causes lameness, so cows eat less and produce less milk. Milk fever (hypocalcemia) usually hits high-yielding cows after calving; the cow goes down and cannot rise. Retained placenta (more than 12 hours after calving) can lead to metritis and infertility. All these issues reduce milk sales. By controlling them, you protect your income. Simple steps like clean bedding, post-milking teat dipping, and regular hoof trimming can prevent most problems. This module will give you practical tools to keep your herd healthy and your milk flowing.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To manage mastitis and other health issues, you need a few basic tools and materials. Most are cheap and available at local agrovet shops or markets. First, for milking hygiene: a clean stainless steel or plastic milking bucket with a lid, a strip cup (a cup with a black mesh screen to detect clumps in milk), and single-use paper towels or clean cotton cloths for drying teats. Never use the same cloth on multiple cows without disinfecting. Second, for teat dipping: a teat dip cup (a small plastic cup that fits over the teat) and a disinfectant solution. Common dips include 0.5% iodine or 4% chlorhexidine. You can also make a dip using 1 part household bleach to 10 parts water, but change it daily. Third, for treating clinical mastitis: antibiotic intramammary tubes (like those containing penicillin or cloxacillin) prescribed by a vet, and a clean syringe for injecting. Always follow the withdrawal period on the labelâusually 3 to 5 daysâbefore selling milk. Fourth, for foot problems: a hoof knife, hoof trimmers, and a foot bath (a shallow trough) filled with 5% copper sulfate solution or 10% zinc sulfate. Fifth, for milk fever: calcium borogluconate 23% injection (400 ml under the skin or into the vein) and a clean 14-gauge needle. Sixth, for general health: a thermometer (digital is best), a stethoscope, and a notebook to record daily milk yield, cow temperature, and any treatments. Seventh, for subclinical mastitis detection: a California Mastitis Test (CMT) kit, which includes a paddle with four cups and a reagent. You can buy a kit for about $10â20. Alternatively, use the strip cup daily. Finally, keep a first-aid box with gloves, antiseptic, and bandages. Store all medicines in a cool, dark place, away from children. Label everything clearly. These tools cost less than the loss from one sick cow, so invest in them early.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to prevent, detect, and treat mastitis and other common dairy health issues. Step 1: Daily observation. Every morning and evening, watch each cow for signs of sickness: off-feed, slow walking, hot udder, or abnormal milk. Use a strip cup to check for clumps, flakes, or blood. Step 2: Pre-milking hygiene. Wash your hands. Use a clean, dry cloth or paper towel to wipe each teat. Discard the first three squirts of milk from each quarter into the strip cup. If you see clumps, that quarter has mastitis. Step 3: Milking order. Milk healthy cows first, then cows with subclinical mastitis (if known), and clinical mastitis cows last. This prevents spreading bacteria. Step 4: Post-milking teat dip. Immediately after milking, dip each teat in disinfectant solution. Do not wipe off. This kills bacteria before they enter the teat canal. Step 5: Treat clinical mastitis. For a hot, swollen quarter with clumpy milk, milk out the quarter completely every 2â4 hours. Insert one intramammary antibiotic tube into the teat canal after milking, as directed by your vet. Massage the udder. Record the cow's temperature. If the cow has a fever (above 39.5Â°C), call a vet for injectable antibiotics. Step 6: Manage foot rot. For a lame cow, clean the hoof with water and a brush. Use a hoof knife to trim away dead sole and expose the infection. Apply a bandage with copper sulfate paste. Put the cow in a dry, clean pen. If severe, give injectable antibiotics (e.g., oxytetracycline) for 3â5 days. Step 7: Treat milk fever. If a cow goes down after calving and cannot rise, give 400 ml calcium borogluconate under the skin. Massage the area. If no improvement in 2 hours, call a vet for intravenous calcium. Step 8: Handle retained placenta. If the placenta is not out 12 hours after calving, do not pull it. Give the cow 50 ml of oxytocin injection and 500 ml of calcium. If still retained after 24 hours, call a vet. Step 9: Record everything. Write down date, cow ID, symptoms, treatment, and milk withdrawal period. Step 10: Review monthly. Count how many cases you had. If more than 2 cases per 10 cows per month, improve bedding and milking routine.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Many farmers lose money because of simple mistakes. Here are the most common ones and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Not using a strip cup. You cannot see clumps in a bucket of milk. Fix: Use a strip cup every milking. It costs $2 and catches mastitis early. Mistake 2: Using a dirty cloth to dry teats. A wet, dirty cloth spreads bacteria from cow to cow. Fix: Use single-use paper towels or a clean, dry cloth per cow. Wash cloths in hot water and disinfectant after each use. Mistake 3: Skipping post-milking teat dip. The teat canal stays open for 30 minutes after milking. Bacteria enter easily. Fix: Dip every teat immediately after milking. Use fresh dip solution daily. Mistake 4: Treating only the visible quarter. Mastitis often affects multiple quarters. Fix: Treat all quarters with intramammary tubes if the cow has clinical signs. Mistake 5: Selling milk during antibiotic withdrawal. This leaves antibiotic residues in milk, which is illegal and harmful. Fix: Read the label. Withdrawal is usually 3â5 days. Discard milk from treated cows. Mistake 6: Ignoring subclinical mastitis. It causes 70% of losses. Fix: Test with CMT every month. Cows with a CMT score of 2 or 3 need treatment. Mistake 7: Rough milking. Squeezing too hard or pulling teats damages tissue. Fix: Use full-hand milking, not thumb-and-finger. Keep a steady rhythm. Mistake 8: Dirty bedding. Wet, manure-filled bedding breeds bacteria. Fix: Add fresh dry bedding daily. Use sawdust, straw, or sand. Clean out wet spots. Mistake 9: Not trimming hooves. Overgrown hooves cause foot rot and lameness. Fix: Trim hooves twice a year. Use a sharp hoof knife. Soak feet in copper sulfate solution every 2 weeks. Mistake 10: Delaying treatment for milk fever. A down cow can die in 24 hours. Fix: Keep calcium borogluconate on hand. Treat immediately. Mistake 11: No records. You forget which cow was treated and when. Fix: Keep a notebook. Write date, cow ID, drug, and withdrawal date. Mistake 12: Using the same needle for all injections. This spreads diseases like anaplasmosis. Fix: Use a new needle for each cow, or sterilize between cows. Fix these mistakes and your herd will be healthier and your milk sales higher.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety is important for you, your workers, and your cows. When handling medicines, always wear gloves. Some antibiotics can cause allergic reactions. Never eat, drink, or smoke while treating animals. Wash your hands with soap after handling drugs. Store all medicines in a locked box, away from children and food. Follow the dosage on the label. Giving too little antibiotic can lead to resistant bacteria. Giving too much can harm the cow. Use a new needle for each injection. For intramammary tubes, clean the teat end with an alcohol swab before inserting the tube. Do not use the same tube for more than one cow. For teat dipping, use a fresh solution every day. Iodine dips can stain, so wear old clothes. Keep the dip cup clean. When treating foot rot, use a hoof knife carefullyâcut away from your body. Wear steel-toed boots when working with cows. For milk fever, calcium borogluconate must be given slowly if injected into the vein. If you are not trained, give it under the skin instead. Watch for signs of shock: rapid breathing, muscle tremors. If they occur, stop and call a vet. Best practice for herd health includes: 1) Vaccinate against common diseases like anthrax and blackleg. 2) Deworm every 3â4 months. 3) Keep a closed herdâavoid bringing in new cows without testing for mastitis and other diseases. 4) Quarantine new animals for 30 days. 5) Provide clean water and balanced feed. 6) Maintain a clean, dry resting area. 7) Milk at the same times every day. 8) Cull cows with chronic mastitis that do not respond to treatment. 9) Train your workers on hygiene and handling. 10) Work with a vet for regular check-ups. Remember: prevention is cheaper than treatment. A healthy cow gives more milk and more profit. Also, respect animal welfareâhandle cows gently. Stress reduces milk let-down and increases disease. Finally, keep a first-aid kit for humans as well: bandages, antiseptic, and gloves. If you get injured, clean the wound and seek medical help. Safety and best practice protect your investment and your family.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: This exercise will help you apply what you learned. Do it over one week with your herd. You will need: a strip cup, a CMT kit (or strip cup only), teat dip, a notebook, and a pen. Day 1: Gather your tools. Wash the strip cup and CMT paddle with hot water. Prepare fresh teat dip solution. Walk through your herd and record each cow's ID, milk yield, and any visible udder swelling. Day 2: During morning milking, use the strip cup on every cow. For each quarter, discard three squirts into the strip cup. Look for clumps, flakes, or watery milk. Record any abnormal quarter. Also check for hot or swollen quarters by feeling. Day 3: If you have a CMT kit, test each quarter. Squirt a small amount of milk into each cup of the paddle. Add an equal amount of CMT reagent. Swirl for 10 seconds. Read the score: 0 (no reaction), 1 (slight slime), 2 (gel forms), 3 (thick gel). Record scores. If no kit, use the strip cup results. Day 4: For any cow with clinical mastitis (clumpy milk, hot udder), treat as follows: milk out the quarter completely, insert an intramammary antibiotic tube, and massage. Record the cow's ID, date, and drug. Mark the withdrawal date on your calendar. For cows with CMT score 2 or 3 but no visible signs, consult your vet for treatment. Day 5: Check all cows for lameness. Lift each hoof and look for swelling, redness, or foul smell. For any lame cow, clean the hoof, trim dead tissue, and apply a copper sulfate bandage. Record. Day 6: Review your records. Count how many cows had mastitis or lameness. Calculate the percentage: (number of cases / total cows) x 100. If above 10%, identify the main cause (dirty bedding, rough milking, etc.). Day 7: Make a plan. Write three actions to improve: e.g., add fresh bedding daily, use teat dip after every milking, trim hooves next month. Share your plan with your workers. Repeat this exercise every month. Over time, you will see fewer cases and higher milk sales. Submit your records to your trainer for feedback. This practical work is the core of herd health management.

quiz.q: What is the most costly disease for small-scale dairy farmers in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Mastitis causes the highest economic losses due to reduced milk yield and quality.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of clinical mastitis?
quiz.explanation: Clinical mastitis shows visible signs like a hot, swollen udder and clumpy milk.

quiz.q: What percentage of total mastitis cost is caused by subclinical cases?
quiz.explanation: Subclinical mastitis causes up to 70% of total mastitis cost because it is hidden.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to detect clumps in milk?
quiz.explanation: A strip cup has a black mesh screen that catches clumps, flakes, or blood.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of iodine for teat dipping?
quiz.explanation: 0.5% iodine is a common and effective teat dip concentration.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for milk after antibiotic treatment?
quiz.explanation: Most intramammary antibiotics require a 3 to 5 day milk withdrawal period.

quiz.q: Which solution is used in a foot bath for foot rot?
quiz.explanation: 5% copper sulfate or 10% zinc sulfate is used in foot baths to treat foot rot.

quiz.q: What is the treatment for milk fever?
quiz.explanation: Calcium borogluconate is given under the skin or intravenously to treat milk fever.

quiz.q: How many hours after calving is a placenta considered retained?
quiz.explanation: Retained placenta is when the placenta is not expelled within 12 hours after calving.

quiz.q: What should you do first before milking each cow?
options: B) Wash hands and wipe teats
quiz.explanation: Pre-milking hygiene includes washing hands and wiping teats with a clean cloth.

quiz.q: Why should you milk healthy cows first?
quiz.explanation: Milking healthy cows first reduces the risk of spreading bacteria from infected cows.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to use a strip cup?
options: A) Fill it with milk from all quarters
B) Discard first three squirts from each quarter
D) Only use it on sick cows
quiz.explanation: Discard the first three squirts from each quarter into the strip cup to check for abnormalities.

quiz.q: How long after milking should you apply teat dip?
quiz.explanation: Teat dip should be applied immediately after milking to kill bacteria before the teat canal closes.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when treating mastitis?
options: B) Treating only the visible quarter
quiz.explanation: Mastitis often affects multiple quarters, so treating only the visible quarter is a mistake.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to sell milk during antibiotic withdrawal?
quiz.explanation: Antibiotic residues in milk are illegal and can cause health problems for consumers.

quiz.q: What is the CMT score that indicates a need for treatment?
quiz.explanation: A CMT score of 2 or 3 indicates subclinical mastitis and requires treatment.

quiz.q: How often should you trim hooves to prevent foot rot?
quiz.explanation: Trimming hooves twice a year helps prevent overgrowth and foot rot.

quiz.q: What should you do if a cow goes down after calving?
quiz.explanation: A down cow after calving likely has milk fever, so treat with calcium borogluconate immediately.

quiz.q: Why should you use a new needle for each cow?
quiz.explanation: Using the same needle can spread blood-borne diseases like anaplasmosis.

quiz.q: What is a sign of foot rot?
quiz.explanation: Foot rot causes lameness, swelling, and foul smell in the hoof.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm your dairy herd?
quiz.explanation: Deworming every 3â4 months helps control internal parasites.

quiz.q: What is the best way to handle a retained placenta?
quiz.explanation: Do not pull; give oxytocin and calcium, and call a vet if it persists beyond 24 hours.

quiz.q: Why is clean bedding important?
quiz.explanation: Wet, dirty bedding breeds bacteria that cause mastitis and foot rot.

quiz.q: What should you do with a cow that has chronic mastitis?
quiz.explanation: Culling cows with chronic mastitis prevents spread and reduces losses.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
options: B) Gather tools and record milk yield
quiz.explanation: The exercise starts by gathering tools and recording each cow's milk yield and udder condition.

quiz.q: How often should you repeat the practical exercise?
quiz.explanation: Monthly monitoring helps track progress and catch problems early.

quiz.q: What percentage of cases should trigger a review of hygiene?
quiz.explanation: If more than 10% of cows have mastitis or lameness, review and improve hygiene practices.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety practice when handling medicines?
quiz.explanation: Wearing gloves protects you from allergic reactions and absorption of medicines.

quiz.q: What should you do before inserting an intramammary tube?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning the teat end with an alcohol swab prevents introducing bacteria into the udder.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of keeping a closed herd?
quiz.explanation: A closed herd avoids bringing in new animals that may carry diseases like mastitis.
